questions.q: In a quantum circuit diagram, what does a single horizontal wire represent?
options: One qubit's timeline, read left to right, with earlier gates drawn to the left of later gates
One classical bit stored permanently alongside the qubits
A physical wire carrying electrical current between gates
The total number of gates used anywhere in the circuit
questions.explain: Each wire is a per-qubit timeline. Position along the wire encodes time: left is earlier, right is later. It is a diagrammatic convention, not a physical conductor.

questions.q: In the diagram q1: ──H──●── / q2: ─────X── (vertical line connecting ● and X), what operation does the dot-and-X combination represent?
options: A CNOT gate with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target
Two independent, unrelated single-qubit gates that happen to be drawn at the same horizontal position
A SWAP gate exchanging qubits 1 and 2
A measurement of qubit 1 that determines qubit 2's starting state
questions.explain: A filled control dot connected by a vertical line to a ⊕/X target symbol is the standard notation for CNOT: the dot marks the control qubit, the X marks the target qubit that gets flipped when the control is |1⟩.

questions.q: Reading q1: ──H──●── / q2: ─────X── left to right and starting from |00⟩, what state results, and how does this compare to Chapter 3's result for H-then-CNOT?
options: (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, exactly matching the state vector [0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071] computed in Chapter 3 for this same gate sequence
(|01⟩+|10⟩)/√2, a different Bell state than Chapter 3 produced
|00⟩ unchanged, since the diagram only shows gate positions, not actual execution
A fully mixed, non-entangled state, since CNOT does not create entanglement by itself
questions.explain: The diagram is just a different notation for the identical H-then-CNOT sequence Chapter 3 already computed. Reading it correctly reproduces the same result: (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, i.e. state vector [0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071].

questions.q: What does a double line (two parallel lines) following a measurement symbol represent in a circuit diagram?
options: A classical bit carrying the measurement's definite 0-or-1 outcome forward through the rest of the diagram
Two qubits that have been merged into a single wire for the rest of the circuit
An error-correction redundancy line with no information content
A second, independent quantum wire added purely for visual symmetry
questions.explain: A single line always carries quantum information (which can be in superposition); after a measurement collapses that to a definite classical outcome, the diagram switches to a double line to show that what follows is a classical bit, not a qubit.

questions.q: Why do real quantum programming tools like Qiskit and Q# represent circuits as diagrams rather than as explicit matrices?
options: Diagrams scale one gate, one qubit at a time, the way code scales, whereas a full circuit's matrix grows exponentially with qubit count and becomes impractical to write or read directly
Matrices cannot represent controlled gates like CNOT at all, so diagrams are the only valid notation for them
Diagrams are required because matrix multiplication only works for single-qubit gates
Real hardware physically only accepts diagrams as input, never numerical data
questions.explain: A circuit's full matrix has dimension 2^n × 2^n, which becomes unmanageable even for modest qubit counts (a 5-qubit circuit's matrix is already 32×32). A diagram instead lists gates per qubit in order, which stays readable regardless of qubit count — matrices remain essential for verifying behavior, just not for authoring or reading circuits.
